paragraphs.text: The other day the ascension of the Life-giver crowned us with a fitting and festal crown, for he lifted up our human nature and planted it in heaven. That was the very beginning of our discourse: that the Saviour gained every gain for us. He bestowed nothing on himself, but granted salvation to us. He made our earthly nature heavenly, and established the dust that the grave devours as a portion of the heavenly natures [?]. The divine apostle knows how to speak of the image of the earthy and the image of the heavenly, and we may hear it in his own words: “The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven.” And he adds: “As is the earthy, so are we who are earthy; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly.” He does not call the first man earthy because he came from the earth, but because he did earthy works. And he does not call the other heavenly because he had his body from heaven, for he took his body from the Virgin and from the earth. He is heavenly because he had virtue in himself and became the body of the Heavenly One. It was called heavenly not by nature, but because of the Heavenly One whom it had put on.

The first man came from the dust and went about doing earthy works. “Dust” is the powder that rises up, while “earth” is what bears fruit. So Paul does not simply call man “earthly”; he calls him “earthy,” because he has fallen under the dust of sins. Just as garments and eyes are harmed by dust, so are souls harmed by sins. When the dust is shaken off, garments and faces become clean. In the same way, when you cast off your sins, souls are cleansed and made light. So blessed David says, “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of those who have been shaken off.” And he says to Jerusalem, “Arise, and shake the dust from yourself.” The heavens take on a form to match the earthy man who is soiled with earthy works: when people are smeared with sins as with dust, the heavens too sift down dust. It is not strange to say that dust is sifted down from heaven. This comes not from any nature of heaven, but from what those who receive it deserve. And who bears witness to these words? God, through Moses, who said: “If you do not listen to the laws of the Lord your God, your rain shall become dust for you, and dust shall come down from heaven. If you do not keep the laws of the Lord your God, your rain shall become dust, and dust shall come down from heaven.” Dust is sifted upon the earthy man, because he is soiled with the dust of sins.

He gives this example about such people, that the heavens rain dust upon the earthy. In the same way God acts fittingly toward each person according to that person's will. If he sees a hard mind, he deals with it according to its hardness; if a soft one, according to its softness. Indeed, many are hard and harsh like iron and bronze. Isaiah says of Israel, “I knew that you are hard; your neck is a sinew of iron, and your forehead bronze.” By “sinews of iron” he means the disobedient neck, which chafes and shrinks from coming under the yoke of godliness and shies away from the laws. As it is said, “Ephraim became a heifer that throws off the yoke, and did not take the yoke.” When people persist in such hardness, disobedience and unbelief, God turns creation to match them: “If you do not listen to my laws, I will make the heaven above you bronze and the earth beneath you iron.” That is, he makes the earth seedless and fruitless.

Creation takes on a form to match the earthy, in order to punish their evils and their contempt for the laws of the Creator. But whoever bears the image of the heavenly—as it is said, “as we have put on the image of the heavenly”—finds the heavens taking on a form to match. For someone whose mind is soft, a rain of sweetness pours down in abundance. Because he has fulfilled the divine commands, God fills his fields with heavenly dew. “Receive the dew of my commands,” he says, “and I will bring you the dew of rain.” If our souls are watered by the divine commands, he also waters our fields with profitable rains. “If you listen to the laws of the Lord your God, the heavens will give their dew and the earth its fruit.” The earth bears fruit for the sake of the obedient.

Let us therefore put on the image of the heavenly. Paul calls the Life-giver heavenly. This is not only because he is from heaven, which is obvious, since God the Word is not only heavenly but also the Lord of heaven and of the angels. It is also because of his flesh, since on earth he practised the virtue of heaven. For if Paul called the Life-giver heavenly only because he is from heaven, how could he call others heavenly too, who did not have their nature from heaven? Blessed David also calls him heavenly, for I find this name used both in the Old Testament and in the New. Paul says, “Let us put on the image of the heavenly,” and David says, “When the Heavenly One sets apart kings upon it.” Upon what? Upon the earth.

When David applied the word “heavenly” to the Life-giver, he was not forcing the words or merely sharing a name. Witnesses agree here in the truth of the facts. Learn it from the order of the passage itself, for David calls the Life-giver heavenly: “When the Heavenly One,” he says, “sets apart kings upon it, they shall be made snow-white in Salmon; the mountain of God, a fat mountain, a mountain made great, a fat mountain.” Since we are applying the name “heavenly” to the Life-giver, I will go through the passage point by point, so that no one may suppose I am forcing invented meanings onto the words. In this way the order of the passage and the words of those who spoke it may proceed clearly and without confusion, and no one will think it forced, but rather truly fitting. “When the Heavenly One sets apart kings upon it,” he says, “they shall be made snow-white.” And what is the Heavenly One's setting apart of kings upon the earth?

Here he calls “kings of the earth” not those who hold worldly honours, but those made radiant with heavenly minds: the saints. Of them Paul says, “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.” Paul does not speak of the kingship of the saints idly, with grandiose words and a profusion of honours that puff up the hearers. One can often say too much, battering the listeners' ears with big talk to unsettle them and lead them to the matter at hand. But Paul does not deceive by talking big. In fact, he cannot even speak worthily of the promises, as he himself testifies: “What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him.” God will give a kingdom to the saints—not an earthly kingdom, but the heavenly one. It is like the kingdom of the Life-giver, who was asked by Pilate, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If it were of this world, my servants would fight for me.” God will give the kingdom to the saints, as Paul says, and Daniel agrees with him: “After that,” he says, “God will raise up a great and mighty kingdom, which will stand and endure forever.” And again: “The saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom.” And here David says, “When the Heavenly One sets apart kings upon it.”

What is this “setting apart”? It means distinguishing and dividing. How will he distinguish the kings? He commanded Paul to be a herald of the kingdom and sent him to preach the kingdom from Jerusalem as far as the regions of Illyricum. He sent one to India, another to the regions of the east, another to the regions of the west, another to the south, and others to the north. “In setting apart” means in distinguishing and dividing: deciding who should be persuaded and by whom, and who would listen to whom and believe. He sent the preachers according to what suited each one. “When the Heavenly One,” he says, “sets apart kings upon it, they shall be made snow-white in Salmon”—that is, they shall be made white. For the preaching of the apostles made the whole world white and showed the earth whiter than snow. It washed the world with the word of truth, wiped it and purified it, according to the saying, “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” Pay attention to the order of the passage: “When the Heavenly One sets apart kings upon it, they shall be made snow-white in Salmon.” Salmon is a Hebrew word that means “peace,” so it is as if he said, “They shall be cleansed in peace.” Having called the Life-giver heavenly, he then foretells his bodily dispensation as well, by calling him a mountain: “the mountain of God, a fat mountain.” He changed the name “heavenly” into the name “mountain.” This does not mean that he himself changed from the truth in any way; rather, in keeping with his dispensation he gathers these names to himself. Our Life-giver is called God, Lord, Creator, Almighty, Heavenly, King and Mountain. Of this mountain blessed Isaiah the prophet says: “In the last days,” says the Lord, “the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God on the tops of the mountains. Many nations shall go and say, ‘Come, let us go to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.’ For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he shall judge among many nations.”

Blessed Daniel also glorified this mountain long before, when he was interpreting the image made of various kinds of materials: gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay. At the end he says that a stone was cut out without hands, struck the image and crushed it, and the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole world. See how words taken in a narrow, literal sense do not fit, except by spiritual interpretation. If he had been speaking of a visible mountain when he said, “The stone became a great mountain and filled the world,” the word “filling” would point to some effect; yet a mountain that comes upon everything does not fill it but covers it. So it is clear that he calls the Life-giver's dispensation a mountain, because it is higher than every other beneficial means: higher than the excellence of the law and the prophets, and higher than that of the inspired speakers who wrote the psalms. “It shall be exalted,” he says, “above all the hills.” And here the Life-giver, speaking of the Church, tells the apostles, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.” What city? The Church. “Jerusalem, built as a city.” The prophet also calls it a house on the tops of the mountains. What house? The Church. But be careful, in case we say one thing for another and force the truth. Let us look for a fitting testimony that the Church is truly called a house. Listen to Paul, writing to Timothy: “so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God.” If the Church is the house of the living God, then the prophet spoke well when he said, “the house of God on the tops of the mountains.” That is, the Church is above all heights. “And many nations shall go” to the house. For many nations do not run to the Jewish [?], but to the Church. “And they shall say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.’” We have often said who the God of Jacob is, according to the sense of the passage: for the God of Jacob appeared as God and man.

Now blessed David says, “When the Heavenly One sets apart kings upon it, they shall be made snow-white in Salmon; the mountain of God, a fat mountain.” He calls the Life-giver's dispensation a fat mountain, meaning rich, strong and full of flowers. For “fat” describes every flower that springs up, as he says in one place, “The beauty of the wilderness shall grow fat,” and again, “These are the sons of fatness.” He calls it a curdled mountain. It gathers what is scattered, fluid and watery, and makes it firm. In the same way, rennet gathers the fluid nature of milk and thickens it, bringing what is soft and spread out into a single whole. After that, the two cannot be separated from what they have been united with, neither the one from the other nor the other from the one. So too Christ, once he has been united with our souls like rennet with milk, is not taken apart or dissolved. Paul's soul was like this. Once it was fluid like milk, but after it was united with Christ he said, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” “The mountain of God, a fat mountain, a curdled mountain.” He calls the Life-giver a fat mountain, just as the Scriptures also call the prophets mountains: “His foundations,” it says, “are on the holy mountains.” And in another place, the same: “You shine wondrously from the everlasting mountains.” He calls the prophets everlasting mountains, as it is said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and brought about salvation for his people, as he spoke by the mouth of the prophets who were from of old.” That is why it says, “You give light wondrously from the everlasting mountains.” “His foundations”—whose? The Life-giver's—“are on the holy mountains,” for the prophetic writings are the foundations of the preaching of the gospel. For this reason the apostle also makes the point plainer when he says, “You are the temple of the living God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, of which Jesus Christ is the cornerstone.” The prophets are called mountains for this reason: a mountain is of the earth yet rises above the earth in height. It comes from the earth and is above it. In the same way the prophets were called mountains, because they came from among men and were above men. The Life-giver too is called a mountain, for he is akin to them according to the flesh, yet by his divinity he surpasses all flesh and every human mind. Because the prophets were called mountains and the Life-giver was also a mountain, people supposed that he was one of the prophets. As he himself says, “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” And they answer, “Some say John the Baptist, some Jeremiah, some Elijah, and some one of the prophets.” They supposed that the holy mountain was one of the prophets. Blessed David said long before, “Why do you suppose, you curdled mountains, that the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell is one of you?” “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They answered and said, “Some say Jeremiah, some Elijah, and some John the Baptist.” Do you see how the prophet foretold their suppositions? “Why,” he says, “do you suppose, you curdled mountains, that the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell is one of you?” And how did he dwell in it? He did not dwell in the prophets in this way, as he says here: “The Lord will dwell in it to the end.” In them he lodged for a time; here he made an everlasting dwelling.

Pay attention to the order of the passage and see how Scripture shows that the same one is heavenly, the same one is a mountain, the same one is God, and the same one is the Saviour of the world. He is one and the same, the one who appeared in the world. For “the Lord,” it says, “will dwell in it to the end,” and then, “The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold.” First he called him heavenly, then a mountain, and then God: “The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold, thousands of guides; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the holy place. He went up on high; he took captivity captive.” The prophet speaks of the one whose chariots are ten-thousandfold, with thousands of guides, who went up on high, took captivity captive and gave gifts to the sons of men. Paul firmly takes up the prophet's meaning and brings it into the sense of the gospel: “To each one grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.” And to this he adds the prophet's testimony, for he says, “He went up on high.” Who is the God who went up? The one whose chariots are ten-thousandfold, with thousands of guides. Who is it who went up? The one of whom he said, “When the Heavenly One sets apart kings upon them.” For he says, “He went up on high and took captivity captive.” Paul sets the passage before us and interprets it himself: “What does ‘he went up’ mean, except that he first went down into the lower parts of the earth? He who went down is the same one who went up above the heavens.” The prophet says, “He gave gifts to men,” and the apostle explains who gave the gifts: “He who went up above the heavens,” he says, “he gave.” As it says “he gave” there, so it says here: “some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists.” See the wealth of the Godhead! See the authority of the glory of the Glorious One! “He gave,” it says. He did not ask; he gave.

He went up on high and took captivity captive. What captivity was there on high? Here “on high” means the cross, as it is said: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” So it is clear that the cross is called “on high,” for on the cross he drew to himself all humanity, which Satan held in exile as a captive. He calls the cross “on high” because on the cross he broke the tyranny of the tyrants and brought the captives back, as it is said: “to proclaim release to the captives.” Christ took those very captives captive. Satan took captives in one way, and Christ in another. Satan led them from freedom into slavery, but Christ led them from slavery into freedom, and from unbelief into faith. Because old custom had taken hold, and the very word “captivity” was dreadful, the world supposed it would be taken captive by the violence of some tyrant. Not knowing the truth, it prepared to fight against the gospel. But the Life-giver concealed the purpose of his love for mankind and advanced as if drawn up for battle. He hurls lightnings at the enemies and rains arrows from the bow of the Spirit, as the apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but mighty, to tear down fortified reasonings and every proud thing raised up against the knowledge of Christ; and we take every mind captive into obedience to Christ.” And because love for mankind stretched the meaning of captivity [?], the world too supposed that he went up on high, to the cross, took captivity captive and gave gifts to men. When men take captives, they plunder their goods. But the great King, conducting his captivity under the banner [?] of his love for mankind, took nothing from the captives; instead he even gave them gifts.

Paul was like this. Once he took others captive, while he was deceived by ignorance; afterwards he was taken captive by the power of Christ. And he openly confessed this good captivity: “Mark, my fair one [?], greets you.” He turned from the bitter captivity and came into the holy captivity. The Life-giver led him about in the bonds of the gospel as a display and an example—not to disgrace him, but to make him glorious. Paul found this captivity so pleasant that he even boasted in its bonds. Listen to him: “I, Paul, an old man and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ, appeal to you.” And elsewhere, with chains upon him, he said, “It is for the hope of Israel that I wear these chains.” And he writes to Timothy, “Share in suffering for the gospel, for which I suffer bonds as a criminal.” But see the boldness of this chosen soul: “But the word of God,” he says, “is not bound. I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they may become imitators of me.”

Do you see what kind of captivity he took captive? “He went up on high,” it says, “and took captivity captive.” From whom? From Satan. For human bodies were Satan's vessels, vessels of every kind. In a house, one vessel is for oil, another for wine, another for vinegar, and another is a vessel of iron or some other material, yet all belong to one master. In the same way Satan took humanity and made vessels of every kind out of it: some vessels of fornication, some of adultery, some of deceit, some of tyranny, some of greed, some of godlessness, some of blasphemy, some of confused speech, some of dishonour. The Life-giver came and saw them all held in pledge. He says to the disciples, “No one can enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods.” He calls Satan strong, not because he was strong against him, but because he was strong against the men who waged war with him. “Unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his vessels.” Do you see that the Life-giver plundered those who had been plundered and took captive those who had been taken captive?

And truly he did what he said. Nowhere do you find the Life-giver setting his hand to teaching people, setting out the details of the word of truth, or drawing anyone into the ways of salvation until he had first bound the slanderer. He took upon himself the life-giving baptism that cleanses all. He mixed the good leaven, his own holiness, with the water, and plunged himself beneath the water to hide the power of the leaven within it. He was baptized, and immediately he goes out from the Jordan into the wilderness to be tempted by Satan. Note this well, I beg you, and see how it agrees with the saying, “No one can plunder the vessels of the strong man unless he first binds the strong man.” Nowhere does the Saviour appear to have taught or performed any sign until he had first bound Satan in the wilderness, and with him all his wickedness. Then, returning from the wilderness, he begins to proclaim the divine messages, and he plunders those whom Satan had plundered—not by his divine power, but by his bodily dispensation. For this was the plan set before him: to conquer Satan through the flesh and not through the Godhead. It would have been a disgraceful battle and victory if God had entered into combat with Satan. But, as I have often said, since the enemy's war was against human beings, he arms human nature in himself against the adversary, so that with the very thing through which it had been wounded it might wound the one who wounded it.

And now, having taken the vessels from him (that is, human souls, which had gone astray, stumbled and wandered about in every kind of evil), he then sends out those same souls, once withered in every evil, as his own vessels, to be adversaries of the very one from whom he took them. Paul the persecutor was also a vessel of evil, an insulter and a fighter against God. He fought against God because he fought against the Son [?], for "whoever denies the Son," it says, "dishonors the Father as well." Notice how the apostle himself lays his former ignorance at his own door [?]: "The saying is trustworthy," he says, "that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost." He takes the fighter against God, the zealot for the Law who in ignorance waged war against Christ, a vessel full of ignorance and zeal, and makes him a chosen vessel. Hear him say to Ananias: "Go, for he is a chosen vessel to me." Do you see how he made a chosen vessel out of a vessel of evil? Elsewhere too Paul calls people vessels: "If God," he says, "wishing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath." By vessels of wrath he means unbelieving souls. "In order to show the greatness of his mercy upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand," that is, us, the vessels of mercy. He is speaking of those who became worthy of his love for humankind and became chosen vessels. This is what "he ascended on high and led captivity captive" means. The Lord himself points to the same thing: "When I am lifted up," he says (that is, when I go up on the cross), "I will draw all people to myself." So he brought those who had been seized back to himself and returned the captives. He freed the exiles and healed the sick. He broke the bonds with which sins had bound them, and in their place he set a crown on the heads of those who had been bound. That sins are bonds, hear the Scripture: "Each one," it says, "is bound in the cords of his own sins." Because he found that sins were bonds, the Lamb of God, who took away the sin of the world, broke the sins. O the love for humankind of our Benefactor and Lord! When a master goes after a runaway slave and catches him, he binds him if he finds him loose. If he finds him healthy, he beats him. If he finds him in the light, he shuts him up in a dark prison. But the Savior went after human nature, which had fled from truth and goodness, from the laws and from the commandments. He found it not loose but bound, and he set it free. He found it naked and clothed it: "As many of you," it says, "as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." He found everyone in prison and brought them out of prison. He found them in darkness and enlightened them: "Land of Zebulun and Naphtali," it says, "the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan: the people that sat in darkness has seen a great light."

And where did he find them bound and set them free? In the error of polytheism, as if in a pit or an underground dungeon. That the pit is the worship of idols, hear Jeremiah the prophet: "The heavens were astonished," he says, "and the earth trembled, for the people has committed two evils. They have forsaken me," he says, "the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cracked cisterns." He calls himself a fountain because a fountain pours out water from its own springs, while a cistern has its water as if begged and brought in from outside. They forsook the true God and were led astray after counterfeits. As Paul says, "When you did not know God, you served beings that by nature are not gods"; you lay bound in the pit of ignorance, in the dungeon of idolatry. That is why David raises his complaint and cries, "Save me from those who go down into the pit." That is also why blessed Isaiah says, "The people that sat in darkness has seen a great light." And because he goes on to explain what gloom they were in, he adds: "the people that sat in darkness and in the shadow of death." The other prophet speaks in the very person of the Savior: "By the blood of your covenant you have released the prisoners from the waterless pit." By the blood of the covenant he means the forgiveness of sins. By prisoners he means people like Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, no longer prisoners of the waterless pit. And how is it by the blood of the covenant? That is the saying: "This is my blood of the new covenant, poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins."

Now pay close attention. David says, "He ascended on high and led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." All the prophets must speak in agreement, for there was one Spirit in all of them. This one says, "You released the prisoners from the waterless pit." Another says, "They will rejoice before you as people rejoice in the days of summer"; the released, he says, will rejoice as at summer. That is why the Savior said, "The harvest is plentiful but the laborers are few. Pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest to work." "Your redeemed," the prophet says, "will rejoice like those who rejoice at the harvest when they gather the fruits of their labors, or like those who divide the spoil." A conqueror takes much spoil in war: gold, silver and clothing. Everything taken is called spoil, because it all lies scattered and jumbled together: clothing, weapons and swords, gold, silver and bread, and whatever else there may be. In the same way Satan had taken everyone and mixed them all together. Christ came and snatched them all from him in a mass: the drunkards, the greedy and the robbers. That is why the prophet says, "They will rejoice before you as people rejoice in summer, and as those who divide the spoil." As David also says, "I will rejoice in your words like one who finds great spoil."

Consider something remarkable. Think of a ruler who wins in the end, binds the rebels and rescues those the rebel had seized. The rebel always pictures death before his eyes, while the exiles rejoice because they have been freed from tyranny and have come into the kingdom. Yet both the rebel who is to die and those who are to be freed are paraded for show, because of the king's victory. In the same way the Giver of Life took Satan and the demons captive in war, together with those whom Satan had seized, and he parades them all together for show. Paul speaks of both: "Christ," he says, "is our peace, who made the two one. He broke down the dividing wall of the fence, the enmity, in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments by his decrees. He canceled the bond of our hostility, took it out of the way and nailed it to the cross. He stripped the principalities and authorities and put them openly to shame." Victors tie a trophy to a pole (a helmet, a breastplate or some other relic of the slain) and carry it around in procession. In the same way he bound Satan's weapons as if to a royal standard and made the demons a public spectacle on the cross. The demons are paraded in mockery and kept for destruction. Even those who had been seized are paraded first, and then they go out into freedom. Hear Paul: "Thanks be to God," he says, "who always leads us in triumph in Christ and spreads through us the fragrance of his knowledge." The rebel is paraded, and so are we who were with the rebel, so that it may be clear who conquered, who the rebel was, and who was with the rebel. He has seized the one and is going to put him to death, while he has rescued and freed the others. So these too must be paraded once, along with the condemned man who is going to his death. Isaiah speaks of such people, paraded and held captive: "The labor of Egypt and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, men of stature, will come over to you. They will walk behind you bound in fetters and will pray to you." To show that they come into this captivity not for their ruin but for their good, he says: "They will walk behind you bound in fetters and will stand praying to you, for God is in you, and there is no God besides you."

The demons are paraded, and the apostles are paraded too. The demons are struck with shame at their defeat, while the apostles proclaim the king's victory. The demons were paraded then, and the heretics are paraded now, who do the work of enemies while posing as members of the household. Just as civil war is the worst of all wars, so the error of the heretics is the worst of all errors. If a pagan insults Christ, I do not find it strange, for he is an enemy of the cross. I take no account of the Jew, for he is an open enemy. But the heretic claims to confess Christ while denying Christ, and professes to preach the Holy Spirit while blaspheming the Holy Spirit. That war distresses me as a war within the household. A fight within a city is worse than any other fight. Worse than any fight in the city is a quarrel within a house. Worse than the strife of city or house is the bitter discord between husband and wife. More grievous still is the smoke that smolders between [mother and children?] [?], and worse yet is the uproar between a stepmother [?] and stepchildren. Consider what enmity within the household is like. Picture a man who comes home from the marketplace and finds wintry gloom [?] on their faces. When it is time for the table and for good cheer, he finds himself in the middle of a war. Cares and sorrows multiply and turn his harbor into a place of storms. He is tossed in his own house as if on the waves of the sea, so that people leave the house and hurry to the marketplace as if it were a harbor. Godly men endured troubles of this kind for Christ's sake, the people Christ spoke of when he said: "Brother will hand brother over to death, and father son, and children will rise up against parents. Son will be divided against father and father against son, mother against daughter, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and a man's enemies will be the members of his own household." Just as war within the house is the most grievous of all wars, so the error of the heretics is the worst of all errors. They seem to belong to the same household and to make the same profession of godliness. They have put on the outward form of godliness, yet they fight against the truth. Of them Paul says that they have the outward form of the truth but have denied its power.

Now if we say the same things again, let no one be annoyed. The point is not that we should say only new things. One may say the same true thing and explain it in a different way. Even when the word is consistent, its explanations are many-sided. God, too, is one, yet he spoke to our fathers through the prophets and the apostles in many portions and in many ways. The same Holy Spirit spoke in the prophets and in the apostles, but that is no reason to shrink from either the former or the latter. Rather, we see one power and diverse operations. When the Father speaks in the prophets, the Son speaks. When the Son speaks in the apostles, the Father speaks. When the Holy Spirit speaks in the prophets and the apostles, the Father and the Son speak. There are no divisions there. One may not cut the uncut nature or divide the indivisible kingdom.

Do you want to know how it is indivisible? Hear God speaking to Moses when Moses hesitated to go to the land of the Egyptians. "I am not fit," Moses says, "to go into Pharaoh's house, for I am weak of voice and slow of tongue. I beg you, Lord, send someone else." When God saw that this hesitation born of weakness was wearying of [?] the command of the one who gave it, he showed Moses who is the craftsman and who is able to fashion the members of the body. He says: "Who gave man a mouth, or who made the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord? I gave a mouth to all, and I can give one to you. I granted it to everyone; shall I deprive you, my prophet, of the gift? Who gave man a mouth? Is it not I, the Lord God?" To Ezekiel he says, "Son of man, behold, I will raise up a horn for all the house of Israel, and I will give you an open mouth." It was not that he was giving him a mouth, for he had one from birth; he calls boldness a mouth. Let us look for this in the Gospel too: who gives the mouth? "When they bring you before tribunals," he says, "do not worry about what you will say, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom." So it is clear that he is the one who said to Moses, "Who gave man a mouth?" and to Ezekiel, "I will give you a mouth." It is he himself who spoke in the old covenant, inspired the prophets and poured his power into the apostles.

Again, Scripture uses the word "lips" to mean not the visible lips but boldness. When David says, "Lord, open my lips," it was not that his lips were shut. He was asking for the boldness he had lost. Otherwise, how could he even say, "Lord, open my lips"? Likewise in the Old Testament: before the languages were confounded there was one language instead of many, and Moses wanted to show that there was one speech and one language. So he says, "The whole earth was one lip." Did all people have a single lip? Surely he called the one speech of the mouth "one lip." "The whole earth," he says, "was one lip and one speech." Clearly, everyone had one speech.

"I will give a mouth and wisdom," he says. Where do we find that he gave it? If we find it given to one person, we will have no doubt about the others. "Some of the Cyrenians and Alexandrians rose up," it says, "and entered into dispute and debate with Stephen." Remember: "I will give a mouth and wisdom, and they will not be able to withstand it." And indeed "they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke." See how God gives a mouth to the prophets, Christ opens the mouths of the apostles, and the Holy Spirit speaks in them.

Someone might think that the Son gives and the Spirit carries out the work, as though giving belonged to one and carrying out the work to another. To prevent this, we must show that the Holy Spirit also gives. In the old covenant God says that he gives, and in the Gospel Christ tells the apostles, "I will give you a mouth." So we must ask whether the one who gives is different from the one who brings the gift. Even now, when kings give gifts, their attendants carry the gift, and the two are not of the same rank. Let us see: perhaps the Son gives, and the Spirit is like an attendant or servant? Learn, then, that just as the Son gives the word to prophets and apostles, so the Spirit is no servant but gives with sovereign authority. It says in the Acts of the Apostles: "When the Holy Spirit came down upon them, they spoke in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." And Paul says, "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one as he himself wills." As he wills, and not as he is ordered. Again, the Savior shows that what he himself gives is also the gift of the Holy Spirit, and what he works is also the working of the Holy Spirit. He says to the apostles: "When they bring you before tribunals, do not worry about what you will say. It will not be you who speak; the Holy Spirit will teach you at that hour what you should say." Do you see that where the Father works, there is the working of the Son and the sovereign authority of the Holy Spirit?

Where there is teaching and enlightenment and discourse on godly religion, no created nature is ever found at work, but only the uncreated nature. Whether in the enlightenment of baptism or in the ineffable mysteries, it is not within an angel's power to enlighten and sanctify. That belongs to the holy, uncreated nature of the Lord. When he speaks in the prophets, it is not some created nature that speaks but the uncreated God [?], as it says: "as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old." But when people must be rescued from afflictions, God sends angels. Whether to rescue from lions or to save from fire, angels serve as ministers of such deliverance. As Paul says, "Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" But the Holy Spirit appears when the mysteries are to be accomplished, when the riches of teaching are to be bestowed, and when the ineffable mysteries of baptism are to be fulfilled.

And let no one's mind ever waver about receiving sanctification through water and the Spirit. Some say: "If the uncreated nature comes to enlighten us in baptism, what need is there of water, which is created? And why did the Savior join the uncreated nature with created nature when he said, 'Unless you are baptized of water and the Spirit, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven'?" Who does not know that water is created? But we must set out the reason why created water is joined with the uncreated Spirit, and for what purpose. I beg you, do not grow weary of listening. Store up the meaning of my words in the storehouses of your minds, so that they do not flow uselessly past your ears. Water spread over the ground does not sink into the earth or water the fields. But when it falls into a channel and runs along the furrows, it is not wasted but irrigates the fields. So now let these words not be scattered; let their meaning water the fields of your mind.

God has given human beings many things, though he himself has no need of what he gives. But because our mortal nature cannot receive invisible gifts, he accustoms it to them through visible things. The Giver of Life could have granted forgiveness of sins without water. The manifestation of the Spirit was enough to wash the guilty, cleanse the defiled, sanctify the unclean and bring the outcast into adoption. But human nature clings somehow [?] to visible things and can receive divine things only feebly and in small measure with the eyes of the mind. So, for the sake of those who cannot rise so high as to see invisible things, he leads them there by an easy path. He set a visible pattern before them, so that by the clear assurance of their eyes their souls might be persuaded of what is invisible. Here is an example. When God took blessed Aaron, the brother of Moses, into his priesthood, he said: "Clothe him in a robe embroidered with mixed threads, made of purple, scarlet, fine linen and blue." Everyone knows what blue, scarlet and purple are. Fine linen is white, like linen cloth. From these four materials and colors they wove the robe. Gold and precious stones were set into it as well. There was the priest's turban on his head, and a gold plate on his forehead, which bears the figure of the Holy Spirit. On the priest's girdle were twelve precious stones: sardius and topaz and emerald, carbuncle and sapphire and jasper, jacinth and agate and amethyst, chrysolite and beryl and onyx. God commanded the twelve stones to be set in place: in the first row the sardius, the topaz and the emerald; in the second the carbuncle, the sapphire and the jasper; in the third the jacinth, the agate and the amethyst; and in the fourth the chrysolite, the beryl and the onyx. On each of the stones he commanded the name of one of the tribes of Israel to be written: on the first the tribe of Reuben, on the second the tribe of Simeon, on the third the tribe of Levi, and all the others in turn. He commanded the girdle to be put around the priest's waist, and the ephod to be fastened over the shoulders and divided at the breast, made of scarlet, fine linen, purple and blue material. "And you shall put two stones on the shoulders," he says, "one on the right and one on the left. On one you shall write the names of six tribes, and on the other the names of the remaining six." Why does he command the names of the sons of Israel to be written twice? Was it not enough to write them on the shoulders? Why on the breast as well? He commands it twice because their minds were so unsteady. Again, he says there are to be flowers shaped like pomegranates at the hem [?] of the robe. Dressed in this way, the priest was commanded to enter the outer sanctuary.

God commanded all this because of their dullness, so that at least through such splendor they might regard the holy things with awe. But a priest's honor does not lie in purple, scarlet, fine linen and blue. It lies in righteousness, as David says: "Let your priests be clothed with righteousness." The garment of righteousness, however, is visible only to the eyes of the mind. God's purpose is not only to help the perfect advance further but to give life to everyone alike. So when people saw the great priest in his godlike splendor, they would reflect that he was the priest of the great God. God wished to show that this robe was not made for any need of his worship but to impress those who saw it. He has no need of it. He seeks simplicity of soul and delights in purity of heart, for to have flourishing virtues within oneself is the true royal purple and the flower of faith. So he commanded Moses that when Aaron entered the Holy of Holies, he was to take off the robe made of fine linen, scarlet, purple and blue, put on a linen robe, and enter the sanctuary that way. Where God looks, there is no need for outward show or for varied robes. Even the robe he had ordered to be made for other purposes, he commanded Aaron to take off. But so that Aaron would not dishonor the sanctuary by the nakedness of his body, God commanded him to put on a linen robe and linen shoes, something plain, without ornate garments. He asks for plainness because that is what pleases God, not finery. Yet, brothers, although he gave Aaron the robe so that onlookers would honor him, he also planted in it a figure of things to come, so that nothing at all would be empty and the hearts of those who came later might be enlightened. Blessed Aaron takes that robe and puts on the whole world at once, like a tunic. For this world is also made of four elements: earth, fire, water and air. From the earth comes the fine linen, the gentlest of them, from the quiet earth. From the sea comes the purple. The scarlet is in the likeness of fire, and the blue is the likeness of the air, for the air is often blue. But let each person take this however he likes, provided he does so with a godly mind.

But let us look at the matter before us: why did he have the names engraved on stones? The priest went in before the altar, while the people stood outside and did not dare to approach. It was a grief that one man alone went in and enjoyed the holy place while everyone else stood outside. So God devised a way to console their troubled minds through the engraved stones. “You cannot go in yourself,” he says; “I will bring you in by the names engraved on the stones.” The priest went in carrying the twelve tribes, and he offered them all to God. The work of the priest is to offer the people to God, for he is the mediator between God and men. He receives blessings from God and passes them on, and he takes the prayers of the people and offers them to God. “The Lord said to Moses,” it says, “Go down and charge the people.” See how he becomes a mediator from God to men and tells the people God’s commands. Again it says that Moses brought the people’s prayers to God and brought God’s commands to the people. That is why the prophet Malachi, when he explained the order of the priesthood, says, “The lips of the priest declare knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord Almighty.” He is called an angel, but not because he has the nature of angels. Scripture calls anyone who carries messages an angel, that is, a messenger. Angels are called angels for this reason: they make God’s will known to the world. The name “angel” does not name a nature. It names a ministry. And because it is a common name, when Saul sent to the prophet, Scripture says that “he sent angels,” that is, messengers, “to tell him the king’s business.” Elsewhere it says that David sent messengers to Abigail, the wife of Nabal, to tell her what David intended.

But the point before us is to show that the priest was a mediator who brought the people to God and bore the people’s weakness. Whoever offers a sacrifice holds it against his breast as he offers it, for that is the posture proper to those who bring gifts. Whoever bears weakness bears it on his shoulders. That is why the names of the people were imprinted on the priest’s shoulder: to teach the priest, “You who are strong must bear the weakness of the weak.” Paul says the same: “You who are strong, bear the weaknesses of the weak.” That priest was a type of Christ. He carried the twelve tribes of Israel by their names, the whole people. Christ does more: he carries the whole world in his own body. He carries it on his breast, for he himself laid humanity upon his breast. To see that he also carries humanity on his shoulder, hear the Lord’s own parable: “Which of you,” he says, “having a hundred sheep, if one of them goes astray, will not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go and look for the one that strayed? If he finds it, truly I tell you, he lays it on his shoulders.” This is also why the Life-giver carries the cross on his shoulder, for by it he lifted up the whole universe. “Jesus went out,” it says, “carrying the cross on his shoulder.” And why on his shoulder? So that Isaiah would not be proved false, who said, “A child is born to us and a son is given, whose government is upon his shoulders.” The priest carries on his breast and on his shoulder, for the work of a priest is to offer the people and to bear the people’s weakness. But let us come to the matter before us.

We brought this up to show why the water is yoked together with the Spirit. There, a robe woven of many colors like flowers was given to the priest. God had no need of the many colors. They were meant to delight the eyes of those who were still under instruction, so that visible glory would urge them on toward what is invisible. In the same way our God knew that the nature of the Spirit is uncreated, so he joined a created nature to that uncreated nature. In this way the eyes of the simple, looking at the water, may see the Holy Spirit as one sees the sun in water. Surely you know that people who cannot look straight at the sun look into water and see it all there? If you could not see by yourself, at least see by means of the water. Here, too, you find that the apostles were not baptized with water. But let no one quibble idly over this. Pay attention to how it turns out. Because the apostles were perfect and received their perfection before the Saviour’s cross, they were not baptized in water. The grace of the Holy Spirit was enough for them.

But our opponents immediately object. “They were baptized,” they say, “and the Saviour bears witness to it. When he heard Peter say, ‘Not only my feet but also my head,’ he said to him, ‘Whoever has been washed has no need to wash.’ So it is clear that he had received baptism.” They do not understand that the baptism of the apostles he spoke of was not the water but the word. “You,” he says, “are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” That by “washed” he meant not baptized with water but enlightened by the word is clear from this: before the passion he says, “Whoever has been washed has no need to wash.” But after the passion, the cross and the resurrection, when he was about to ascend, the disciples gathered together and asked him, “Lord, when will you restore the kingdom to Israel?” He said to them, “It is not for you to know the times or the hours that the Father has set by his own authority; but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you.” And what does he say after that? “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized.” He did not say, “You have been baptized.” He said this after the resurrection. Before the resurrection he had said “washed.” If they had been baptized before the passion, he would not have said to men already enlightened, “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” And why “not many days from now”? Because he ascended when the forty days after the resurrection were complete, and ten days later, when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, the Holy Spirit appeared. So the Life-giver fittingly said, “You will be baptized not many days from now,” that is, after ten days. “You,” he says, “will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” He did not say “with water” but “with the Spirit,” because for one who has been perfected and sanctified, communion with the Spirit alone is enough. “When,” it says, “the Holy Spirit came and filled the house where they were sitting,” there was no water anywhere there. This makes it plain that where divine power appears, there is no need of any action or matter. The Spirit is enough to complete the enlightenment, even without water.

Yet God does not want the tradition of the mysteries to be despised on the pretext of perfection. So you must not say, “Since I can attain it with my mind, what need is there for the baptism of water?” Our purpose here has been to show that God is able to give his gifts and graces even without water. He is able to enlighten without water, but we are not able to receive enlightenment without water. And since the Saviour’s way of training was meant for our instruction, we must bear in mind that even if we are perfect, no one is more perfect than Christ. The Life-giver wanted to remove every pretext and leave you no excuse for fleeing from the water, so he himself was baptized first in the river Jordan. But let us come back here to the matter before us.

When the Spirit rests upon a person, it baptizes him even if he has not yet been baptized in water. I do not mean only the apostles. In the house of Cornelius, too, while Peter was still speaking, the Spirit came and rested upon Cornelius and his household. This did not happen without reason. The Holy Spirit knew that Peter had scruples and was slow to baptize those who came from the Gentiles. At that time the apostles thought that the grace of Christ had been given only to the Jewish people, so they shrank from giving baptism to those from the Gentiles and had scruples about it. The divine Spirit wanted to show that human minds have no power to hold back God’s gift. So it rested upon them before baptism, before they were instructed and enrolled. When Peter saw that the Spirit had come down and was resting on them, he said, “Can I withhold the water from these people, who have already received the Holy Spirit, just as we did without water?” Later the same Peter explained the circumstances of the matter to the apostles in Jerusalem. They had scruples about him and said, “You went in to Gentiles and ate and drank with them.” Peter set out his defence in order before them and said, “I was in the city of Joppa, and they summoned me there. While I was speaking the word to them, the Holy Spirit came and rested upon them, and I remembered the word of the Lord, which he spoke: ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’”

Do you see how water was given for a necessary purpose, to make human minds firm? Whoever is to be enlightened is twofold, made of body and soul. The nature of the soul is invisible, and the body is a visible structure. So God gave a twofold gift, one for each part: water, manifest and visible, for the body, and the invisible gift of the Holy Spirit for the hidden soul of the person. Think of a king’s grants. They are given both by a living hand and by lifeless instruments, for the reed pen and the ink are dead tools while the king’s hand is alive. Yet although the king’s hand needs the reed and the ink, that does not make them equal in honour to the king’s hand. In the same way, even if water is needed, like ink, so that the divine writing may be imprinted by means of the visible water, is the water therefore equal in honour to the Spirit? No. We must understand it like this: the Holy Spirit writes its benefaction by means of the water. People often presented written petitions to kings. While the document is still in the hands of those presenting it, it is called a petition. When the king sets his hand to it, it is called a deed of grant. Before the king puts his signature on it, it is a sheet of paper still worth ten pennies. When the king sets his hand to it and confirms it, it is worth many weights of gold. What was cheap becomes precious, and what used to sell for little is now valued at a great price. Although it was given freely, the grace has shown the measure of the benefaction. There the paper, the ink and the reed are of little value until the king sets his hand to them. Once the king has confirmed it, you no longer look at the paper and the reed but at the gift of the king’s hand that wrote it. So too when you see the water by itself, know that it is not worth a single small coin. But if you see the Spirit come down and resting upon the waters, you will understand that the invisible [?] of sovereign power is there through the Lord’s grace, and that the water you see is the instrument of invisible grace.

That is why there is water: not to be counted alongside the Spirit, but to lead you toward the invisible. Where an invisible nature calls people to itself, a visible mediator is needed, so that through the visible they may draw near to the invisible. Let me bring in an ancient example. The Law proclaimed God, but he was invisible, as God is. He gave a law, and so that the visible law would not teach them to despise the invisible [?], Moses became the mediator between God and men. Those who could not see God would look at Moses’ face and through him see the invisible. Moses is yoked with God, not as an equal in honour, but as a mortal whose face could guide people toward the immortal nature. They believed God together with Moses, and Moses together with God. Moses was not to be believed apart from God, for no one would put faith in a man. Nor was God to be believed apart from Moses, for without a mediator mortal nature could not be led. That is why the blessed Paul says that the law was given, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. And the mediator between God and the people was Moses.

And see something remarkable. Scripture says, “The people believed in God and in Moses his servant.” Because it said that the people believed in God and in Moses, is Moses then equal in honour to God? If Moses, though counted together with God, is not his equal in honour, [neither is the water] equal in honour to the Holy Spirit [?]. Elsewhere Scripture says, “All the people feared the Lord and Samuel.” Because it said that they also feared Samuel, is Samuel equal in honour to God? No. They feared the one as Lord and the other as mediator. In the same way, when you hear of the mystery of water and Spirit, think of the sovereignty of the Spirit as true gift, as uncreated grace, as an unending kingdom. When you see the water, recognize that the visible is mediating toward the invisible, divine nature. It is just as when the people believed Moses and God, and feared the Lord and Samuel. And elsewhere it says, “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon.” Gideon was their general and God their protector, so it says, “the sword of the Lord and of Gideon”: of the one as king and of the other as mediator.

I say all this so that you will not think about these things at random and in confusion, and so fail to recognize the different aspects of the meaning of words and things. People who mix up such words, names and ranks are like someone who mixes many different materials together, as if one were to melt gold, silver, iron, copper and lead into one mass. In the same way, a person whose mind is confused and who cannot tell things apart is not acceptable even when he offers a sacrifice. As God himself says, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; its turning shall be to you.” It is not enough to offer rightly; one must also divide rightly. What does it mean to divide? It means to understand the authority of the Spirit and to recognize the mediation of the water. But if you mix everything together, Moses with God, Samuel with the Lord, the water with the Holy Spirit, you will end up with many materials mixed together. As God himself says: “Son of man, the house of Israel have mixed copper and lead and iron. Therefore say: Because they have mixed gold and silver and iron and lead together, behold, I will take you in as into a smelting furnace, and I will melt you down into purity, and you shall no longer be mixed.”

“But,” they say, “we do not find the Holy Spirit presented as a divine authority. We find it presented as a gift of royal bounty. For it is written that the Holy Spirit is an anointing: ‘Jesus of Nazareth,’ it says, ‘whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.’ Is the Spirit God, then? Look, it is an anointing. The anointing is one kind of thing and those who are anointed are another. In the same way,” they say, “God, who anointed, has one being, and the Spirit, which is the anointing, has another nature.” The heretics are eager only to count names, not to examine the meaning. They drag words this way and that and use human reasoning to corrupt the order of true religion. So let us give them an answer: “You yourself say that the anointing has one nature and those who are anointed another. Then you must also admit that the fisherman has one nature and the fish another, the garment one nature and the weaver another, shepherding one nature and the sheep another, the vinedresser one and the vineyard another. Will each of these not appear distinct from the other?” Now pay attention. The Life-giver says to the apostles, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” The apostles are fishers, and those caught in the net are men. So let the heretic say it: just as fish have one nature and men another, do men have one nature and the apostles, the preachers, another? Just as the fisherman has one nature and the fish another, do the learners have one nature and the teachers another? Who would accept such ravings and nonsense, without knowing that the teachers belonged to this world and the learners came from among men? The apostle also says, “You are God’s building, God’s field.” Do you not know that the building has one nature and the builder another? And again: “Like a master builder I laid the foundation.” If Paul was the master builder and they were the building, did the master builder and the building have different natures? If you follow the words alone, see how far the error spreads. The apostle says again, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Here we see that the planter has one role and the one who waters another, and again that the planter is one thing and the plant another. Was Paul, who planted, of one nature, and the Corinthians, whom he planted, of another? Why do you stumble over the words and not look to the meaning? The Holy Spirit is called an anointing so that a visible name may proclaim invisible grace. In former times kings were anointed with holy oil from the horn, and priests and prophets too. But the Holy Spirit, which came down and rested upon the Life-giver as a pattern for us and not out of any need, appeared without oil. Afterward, too, it enlightened many without water and anointed many without oil. And note this, I beg you: when the Holy Spirit wants to show its works, it anoints even without oil. Where did Moses get the power to anoint Aaron, when he himself had not been anointed? Because Moses was perfect, the Holy Spirit came to rest on him without oil. It was in Moses, and so he had no need of oil. Likewise the apostles baptized with water and the Spirit, though they themselves were baptized not with water but with the Spirit. So too Moses, who had been anointed not with oil but with the Spirit, anointed Aaron with the holy oil.

It is called an anointing for many purposes. The human race fell sick, and disease seized the whole world. He came and found the whole world paralysed. He anoints our nature to heal it of its pains. He anoints it to train it for the fight against Satan. What oil is to the athlete who wrestles, the power of the Spirit is to those who contend against Satan. He calls the Spirit an anointing to show that he has restored our diseased and mortal nature to immortal glory.

It is also called a gift. The heretics say, “The Spirit is God’s gift, for Scripture itself says that God gave the Holy Spirit to those who humble themselves before him. The giver is one thing and the gift is another.” If you call the Spirit a gift because it was given, then call the Son a gift too, for the Son was also given: “God so loved the world,” it says, “that he gave his only Son.” He gave the Spirit and he gave the Son, so both are gifts. Can you deny that the Son is God because he was called the Father’s gift? No. He is a gift by the dispensation and God by natural dignity. In the same way the Holy Spirit is God by authority, and a gift because it is imparted through the mystery. Whatever is given is a gift, but that gift often turns out to be a giver as well. God gave his only-begotten Son, and he was called a gift. Yet the gift is in turn a giver: “He went up on high,” it says, “and led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men.” He gave, and he was given. He gave as God, and he was given as man. But let this be enough for now.

I know I have made my discourse long. I did not do it to please myself but to satisfy your longing. You have always longed to know how the slander that they cast on the Holy Spirit might be cleared away, for you are friends of the Father, beloved of the Son, and longing for the Holy Spirit. Do not be surprised that I call servants friends. You are servants by nature and friends by grace. Hear the Lord himself: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends.” The Lord did not disdain to call us friends, so shall we disdain it? That is why Ananias and his companions said, “Have mercy on us for the sake of Abraham your servant and Isaac your beloved,” and David said, “Your friends, O God, have become very precious to me.”

Let us say this with boldness; let every mouth proclaim it. The mouths of the prophets have been entrusted to us, though we are not worthy of the prophets. The mouths of the apostles have been entrusted to us, though we come nowhere near the apostles. Even so, we must not cast away the honour entrusted to us. We must sharpen our tongues, not to slay unbelievers but to turn unbelief around and set it right. A bold mouth belonged especially to the prophets. A bold mouth was the special mark of the apostles, who were firm pillars of true religion: mouths that were opened and never shut. As Paul says, “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians.” Mouths opened: “To you,” it says, “I will give an open mouth.” Our mouths too have been opened, for we are the mouths of right glorification against heretical error. They have been opened and will not be shut. Even if our words fall silent, their fruits do not cease, for God knows those who are to be saved and recognizes those who are to turn back. Those who speak do not know whose hearts their words enter. Does that mean God does not know those who are about to fall into the catch?

The word of preaching is a net. The fisherman [?] his cast and throws out the net. He knows that he has cast it, but he does not know what it has caught, because the tool does its work hidden in the depths of the water. In the same way, when the cast of the divine word is drawn into hidden souls, the speaker does not know who has fallen into the net. But God, who inspects the net, knows which fish has been caught. He knows which of those who fight against the Spirit the teaching about the Spirit’s divinity has brought into the net, and which of the Arians the glory of Christ has drawn in. God stands and examines minds and watches the working of the cast. Let me use yet another illustration. When fishermen cast a net, they stand far apart from one another and close the net around the fish like a wall, so that a bay of water in the middle is enclosed by the net. When they want to haul it in, those standing apart gradually come closer to each other, until the two sides of the net come together and are joined end to end. In the same way, in the first era, while the two sides were still apart, God appointed the prophets to haul the net, and in the second era the apostles. The prophets hauled the net with the old, and the apostles with the new. Two bands of fishermen, one on each side, enclose a single bay between them. The bay in the middle is the east, opposite it are the west and the south, and facing it is the north. Hear the Lord himself: “They will come,” he says, “from east and west, from the north and from the sea, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.” In that bay, in that same gulf, ordinary fishermen catch fish for their destruction, but these catch them for salvation. The two sides come together, the fishermen are found to share one nature and one craft, and those who were apart are joined to one another. So too at the end of this world, when the time comes [?] to haul in the net, the prophets will run up and show their labours and how much they hauled, and the apostles their toils and how much they brought into the net.

That same net has been cast now as well, and it is drawn not by any hand of ours but by the apostolic right hand. If I say anything from my own mind, do not accept it unless Paul says it, unless Isaiah bears witness to it. The hand of the prophets draws the net, and now the right hand of the apostles spreads it out. But there is another comparison to be seen here too. When a net is cast, the fish darts away [?] and heads for the middle of the enclosure; and many times it leaps [?] right out of it, as the disciples of the heretics do now. And see the wonder: at first Satan cast a net over the world, and the demons drew it, but the righteous darted away [?] and got out beyond the net, as David says: “By my God I shall leap over a wall.” From Babylon too Satan drew his net, to make a catch [?] of everyone; but the three holy fish sped past the net as if on wings [?], and with the prophet, it is written, they said: “Let sinners fall into their own nets.” And since Satan, who said, “I have roamed and gone about under heaven, and here I am,” had cast an evil net over the world, Christ came and spun a snare [?] against him. Through the apostles he drew nets for those who were to be caught out of Satan's grasp, and he brought the whole world within his net. What then? Are we inventing anything from our own minds? Listen to the Lord himself: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net that is cast into the sea and gathers from every side.” May it be granted to all of us to fall within that net and to be found in that catch. And the wonder is this: one who today falls into the net like a fish, tomorrow, like a fisherman, catches other fish. There, fish that fall into the net go from life to death; here, those who fall within the net are gathered from death into life. That is why the Life-giver said to Peter, “Cast your net on the right side,” and he gathered a great many fish. He teaches that through visible things we must proceed to the understanding of things perceived by the mind. For in this very connection he says, “Do not be afraid, Peter; from now on you will catch men for life,” that is, you will win them for eternal life.

From now on, then, may it be granted to all of us to fall within the net of right glorification, to dwell in the holy enclosure of the faith, and to hold within ourselves faith in the Trinity, the faith of the three patriarchs. For the heavenly Trinity is in heaven, and the three patriarchs are on earth. The nature of the one is not belied, nor is the honor of the other denied. This trinity is divided by time and separated by place; but that one, timeless and eternal, reigns forever, saves always, and enlightens without ceasing. Through it may all of us be saved in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever.
